sections.b: In Numbers 11–21 Moses is at his most human. He tells God he cannot carry the people "alone" and asks to die (Numbers 11:11–15). He shares his spirit with seventy elders and wishes all God's people were prophets (11:29). God defends him against Miriam and Aaron as the one he speaks with "mouth to mouth" (12:6–8), and the narrator calls him the humblest man on earth (12:3). Twice he talks God out of destroying Israel (14:13–19; 16:22). Then at Meribah he strikes the rock and calls the people rebels, and God bars him from the land (20:10–12). Readers still debate what his sin was.
sections.refs: Numbers 11:11–29; Numbers 12:3–8; Numbers 14:11–20; Numbers 16:4, 22; Numbers 20:7–13; Deuteronomy 1:37; Psalm 106:32–33

sections.h: "Very humble" and the question of authorship
sections.b: Numbers 12:3 praises Moses' humility in the third person. Jewish and Christian tradition, holding that Moses wrote the Torah, explained it as written at God's direction or added by a later inspired hand. Critical scholars treat it as clear evidence of a later author. The verse is often cited in debates over who wrote the Pentateuch. Some modern readers also note that "humble" (anav) can mean "afflicted" or "burdened," which fits Moses' complaint in chapter 11.

common: Moses was kept out of the promised land because he struck the rock instead of speaking to it.
uncommon: Moses' sin at Meribah was calling the people "rebels" in anger (Maimonides), or saying "we" as if he gave the water (Ramban).

sections.b: Aaron joins Miriam in criticizing Moses, confesses, and pleads for her (Numbers 12:1–12). Korah attacks his priesthood, and God confirms it twice: by fire on the 250 who offered incense and by Aaron's staff that blooms with almonds (16:35; 17:8). When plague breaks out, Aaron runs into the crowd with incense and "stood between the dead and the living" (16:48). He shares Moses' failure at Meribah (20:12, 24) and dies on Mount Hor after his garments are put on his son Eleazar (20:22–29). All Israel mourns him thirty days, and the rabbis remembered him as a lover and pursuer of peace.
sections.refs: Numbers 12:1–12; Numbers 16:46–50; Numbers 17:1–11; Numbers 18:1–20; Numbers 20:12, 22–29; Numbers 33:38–39; Mishnah Avot 1:12

sections.b: Miriam leads the complaint against Moses over his Cushite wife and over his unique authority (Numbers 12:1–2; the Hebrew verb is feminine). She is struck with a skin disease and shut out of the camp for seven days, and the whole people waits for her (12:10–15). Deuteronomy 24:9 tells Israel to remember it. She dies at Kadesh (20:1), and in the next verse there is no water, which gave rise to the Jewish tradition of Miriam's well, said to have traveled with Israel for her sake.

uncommon: African American interpreters such as Cain Hope Felder and Randall Bailey read Numbers 12 as God defending a Black woman's marriage against prejudice.

sections.b: Korah, a Levite of the clan of Kohath, joins Reubenites Dathan, Abiram and On, and 250 leaders, and tells Moses and Aaron, "Enough of you! The whole community is holy" (Numbers 16:3). Moses proposes a test with fire pans of incense. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come and call Egypt "a land flowing with milk and honey" (16:13). The earth swallows the rebels' households, and fire from the LORD consumes the 250 (16:31–35). Critical scholars see a story of a lay revolt (Dathan and Abiram) woven with a Priestly story about the priesthood (Korah and the 250).

The Mishnah calls Korah's quarrel the model of a dispute "not for the sake of heaven" (Avot 5:17), and a midrash has him mock the law of tassels (Numbers Rabbah 18:3). Jude 11 lists Korah's revolt with Cain and Balaam as a pattern for false teachers. The "sons of Korah" survived (26:11), and eleven psalms carry their name, among them Psalms 42, 46, 84 and 88.
sections.refs: Mishnah Avot 5:17; Jude 11; 2 Timothy 2:19; Psalm 42; Psalm 46; Psalm 84; 1 Chronicles 6:22–28

sections.b: Caleb hushes the crowd and says Israel can take the land at once (Numbers 13:30). With Joshua he tears his clothes and pleads that the land is "a good land, very, very good" (14:7). God singles him out: "my servant Caleb had a different spirit with him, and he followed me fully" (14:24). He and Joshua alone of the scouts survive (14:38). The Talmud imagines him getting the crowd's attention by pretending to join the complaint (Sotah 35a).

Joshua appears as Moses' zealous assistant who wants Eldad and Medad stopped (Numbers 11:28). Moses renames him from Hoshea, "he saves," to Yehoshua, "the LORD saves" (13:16), the Hebrew form of the name Jesus. He is the scout from Ephraim, and with Caleb he urges trust in God (14:6–9). Only these two of their generation will enter the land (14:30, 38).

The scouts return to Moses at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Paran (Numbers 13:26). Israel is back there in the fortieth year: Miriam dies, the water runs out, and Moses strikes the rock (20:1–13). From Kadesh Moses sends messengers to Edom (20:14–16). The pun is part of the story: at Kadesh, "holy place," Moses fails to "treat God as holy," and God "showed himself holy" (20:12–13). Excavations at Tell el-Qudeirat found Israelite forts of the 10th to 6th centuries BC but nothing from earlier.

The heifer must be red, without defect, and never yoked. It is slaughtered outside the camp before Eleazar, its blood is spattered toward the tent seven times, and it is burned whole with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn (Numbers 19:1–6). The ashes, mixed with running water, are sprinkled on anyone defiled by a corpse on the third and seventh days (19:11–19). Everyone who prepares or handles them becomes unclean until evening. The rite is called a sin offering (19:9), which Milgrom explained as a purification offering that absorbs impurity.

The rabbis made it the classic chok, a statute whose reason is hidden. A midrash says even Solomon could not understand it (Numbers Rabbah 19:3). Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai told his students: "The dead do not make unclean, nor does water make clean. It is the King's decree" (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 4:7). The Mishnah tractate Parah says only seven or nine heifers were ever prepared, and Maimonides wrote that the tenth will be prepared by the Messiah.

Hebrews 9:13–14 argues from the lesser to the greater: if the ashes of a heifer made the defiled outwardly pure, how much more will the blood of Christ purify the conscience. Hebrews 13:11–13 adds that Jesus, like the sin offerings, suffered "outside the gate." The Epistle of Barnabas 8 and many later Christian writers read the heifer as a figure of Christ.

common: A red heifer must be born before a Third Temple can be built in Jerusalem.
uncommon: The heifer's ashes work like a detergent that absorbs impurity, which is why they defile those who handle them (Milgrom).

sections.b: When the people complain against God and Moses, "burning" snakes (seraphim) bite them and many die. After they confess, God tells Moses to make a "burning one" and put it on a pole. Moses makes a snake of bronze, a play on words (nachash nechoshet), and whoever is bitten looks at it and lives (Numbers 21:4–9). God does not remove the snakes; he gives a way to survive them.

Jewish tradition insists the image had no power of its own. The Mishnah asks, "Could a snake kill or give life?" and answers that Israel was healed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven (Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–7 says, "The one who turned to it was not saved by the thing he looked at, but by you, the Savior of all." Centuries later Hezekiah smashed it, because people burned incense to it and called it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4).
sections.refs: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8; Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–12; 2 Kings 18:4

sections.b: Jesus tells Nicodemus that the Son of Man must be "lifted up" as Moses lifted up the snake, so that everyone who believes may have eternal life (John 3:14–15). John uses "lifted up" for the cross (John 12:32–33). Barnabas 12 and Justin Martyr develop the comparison, and it remains a favorite Christian image of salvation by looking in faith. Jewish readers, by contrast, stress that the cure came from God and not from the bronze.

Snakes stood for healing and life across the ancient world. At Timna, a copper-mining valley in the Arabah, Beno Rothenberg found a small copper snake with a gilded head in an Egyptian shrine to Hathor. In the later 12th century BC the shrine was turned into a tent shrine, apparently by Midianites. Many scholars think the Nehushtan tradition came from this world; others warn that the find shows only that such objects existed.

common: The bronze snake is the source of the medical symbol of a snake on a staff (that symbol is actually the Greek rod of Asclepius).

claude.title: The cure in the shape of the curse
claude.body: The healing image is shaped like the thing that is killing them. My suggestion is that the story teaches Israel to face the cause of death under God's command, not to flee it. Paul says Christ "became a curse" (Galatians 3:13) and God "made him sin" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Preachers often link those lines to the snake. Reading Numbers 21 itself this way is my own emphasis.

sections.b: Israelites are to put tassels on the corners of their clothes, with a cord of blue-violet (tekhelet), so that they "remember all the LORD's commands" and do not "go scouting" after their own hearts and eyes (Numbers 15:37–41). The verb tur is the one used for the twelve scouts. Deuteronomy 22:12 repeats the command. The passage became the third paragraph of the Shema.

sections.h: Tassels in Jewish and Christian life
sections.b: Jews wear tsitsit on the tallit (prayer shawl) and on a small garment under their clothes. The blue dye, from a sea snail, was lost for centuries; some now use a dye from the banded dye-murex. In the Gospels a sick woman touches the edge, probably the tassel, of Jesus' cloak (Matthew 9:20; 14:36), and Jesus criticizes those who make their tassels long for show (Matthew 23:5).

Sihon refuses Israel passage and attacks at Jahaz; Israel takes his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, including his capital Heshbon (Numbers 21:21–26). An old poem, the Song of Heshbon, celebrates the fall of Moab to Sihon (21:27–30), and Jeremiah 48:45–46 reuses it. Og of Bashan then fights at Edrei and is defeated (21:33–35). Deuteronomy 3:11 calls Og the last of the Rephaim, with an iron bed nine cubits long.

The two kings became a stock example of God's help: Joshua 2:10 (Rahab has heard of them), Judges 11:19–22 (Jephthah's argument with Ammon), Nehemiah 9:22, Psalm 135:10–12 and Psalm 136:17–22. Archaeologists found no Late Bronze Age city at Tell Hesban, the usual site of Heshbon, only an Iron Age I village, and scholars read the evidence in different ways (see the date of the exodus). Some date the story later, and some look for Sihon's Heshbon at another site, such as Tell Jalul.

In Numbers 11 the people complain, "We have nothing to look at but the manna!" (11:6). The narrator answers with a description of how good it was: like coriander seed, the look of bdellium, tasting like a cake made with rich oil (11:7–9). In 21:5 they call it "this flimsy food." The Talmud says it tasted like bread to young men, like oil to the old and like honey to small children, and that it was absorbed without waste (Yoma 75b).

sections.h: The spirit on the seventy elders
sections.b: God takes some of "the spirit that is on" Moses and puts it on seventy elders, who prophesy (Numbers 11:16–17, 25). Eldad and Medad receive it in the camp, and Moses says, "If only all the LORD's people were prophets, if only the LORD would put his spirit on them!" (11:29). Joel 2:28–29 turns the wish into a promise, and Peter quotes Joel at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18).

sections.h: Moses and Aaron pray for the people
sections.b: Numbers 11–21 is full of intercession. Moses prays and the fire at Taberah stops (Numbers 11:2). He cries out for Miriam (12:13). When God offers to destroy Israel and start over with him, he refuses and quotes God's own words, "slow to anger and great in loyal love" (14:13–19), and God says, "I have forgiven" (14:20). Moses and Aaron plead, "when one man sins, will you be angry with the whole community?" (16:22). Aaron runs with incense into the plague and stands "between the dead and the living" (16:48). Moses prays for the people bitten by snakes (21:7).
sections.refs: Numbers 11:2; Numbers 12:13; Numbers 14:13–20; Numbers 16:22, 46–48; Numbers 21:7; Psalm 106:23, 30

sections.h: The generation that missed the rest
sections.b: The scouts' report and the people's refusal (Numbers 13–14) are the background of Psalm 95:8–11, where God swears "they will not enter my rest." Hebrews 3:7–4:11 builds on this: the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, so a rest remains for God's people, and readers must not harden their hearts. Paul also uses the wilderness deaths as a warning to the church (1 Corinthians 10:5, 10).

sections.h: Glory at the moment of revolt
sections.b: In Numbers the glory of the LORD appears at moments of rebellion: when the people are about to stone Joshua and Caleb (14:10), at Korah's challenge (16:19, 42), and at the waters of Meribah (20:6). In the middle of judgment God swears that "the LORD's glory will fill all the earth" (14:21). The glory that once filled the new tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) now comes to judge and also to save, since Moses prays each time it appears.
sections.refs: Numbers 14:10, 21–22; Numbers 16:19, 42; Numbers 20:6; Isaiah 6:3; Habakkuk 2:14; Exodus 40:34

sections.b: Korah's revolt asks who may serve at the altar. God answers by fire, by Aaron's blooming staff, and by a charter in Numbers 18. The priests guard the holy things and "bear the guilt of the sanctuary"; the Levites are "joined" to them as guards of the tent; outsiders who come near die (18:1–7). The priests receive offerings, firstfruits and firstborn as "a covenant of salt," and no land: "I am your portion" (18:19–20). Milgrom read the system as a protective ring around the holy.

Numbers 18:21–32 gives Israel's whole tithe to the Levites as wages for their work at the tent, and requires them to give a tenth of it, the best part, to the priests. Deuteronomy 14:22–29 describes a tithe the family eats at the sanctuary, and a third-year tithe for the poor; the rabbis counted a "first tithe," a "second tithe" and a "poor tithe" to fit them together. Nehemiah 10:37–39 renews the Levites' tithe after the exile.

Contact with a corpse, a bone or a grave, or being in a tent where someone died, makes a person unclean seven days, the strongest of all impurities. Cleansing needs the water mixed with the red heifer's ashes, sprinkled on the third and seventh days. One who refuses defiles the sanctuary and is cut off (Numbers 19:11–22). Jesus touches the dead to raise them (Luke 7:14), and the priest and Levite in his parable may have been avoiding corpse impurity (Luke 10:31–32).
sections.refs: Numbers 19:11–22; Numbers 5:2; Numbers 6:6–12; Leviticus 21:1–4; Luke 7:14; Luke 10:31–32

sections.b: Numbers 15:32–36 tells of a man found gathering wood on the Sabbath. He is held until God rules, and the community stones him outside the camp. Placed right after the law on sins "with a high hand" (15:30–31), the story shows defiant sin. Rabbi Akiva identified him as Zelophehad (Shabbat 96b). Christians often set the story beside Jesus' teaching that "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings" (Mark 2:27).

Because the people refused the land after the scouts' report, God decrees forty years in the wilderness, "a day for a year" for the forty days of scouting (Numbers 14:33–34). The adults counted in the census will die there; their children will enter. The thirty-eight years between chapters 14 and 20 pass almost in silence. By 20:1 Israel is back at Kadesh in the fortieth year, and the leaders of the exodus begin to die.
sections.refs: Numbers 14:26–35; Numbers 20:1, 22–29; Numbers 33:19–38; Deuteronomy 2:14; Psalm 95:10; Acts 7:36

sections.b: At Arad, Israel vows to "devote" the Canaanite towns to destruction if God gives victory, and names the place Hormah (Numbers 21:1–3). The same word is used of Sihon's and Og's peoples in Deuteronomy 2:34 and 3:6. Israel was not alone in this language: the Moabite king Mesha boasts on his stele of devoting the town of Nebo to his god. Numbers 18:14 shows the other side of cherem: devoted things belong wholly to God.
sections.refs: Numbers 14:45; Numbers 18:14; Numbers 21:1–3, 35; Deuteronomy 2:34; Deuteronomy 3:6; Leviticus 27:28

sections.b: Moses asks Edom to let Israel pass on the King's Highway, calling Israel "your brother" and promising to pay for water (Numbers 20:14–19). Edom refuses and comes out armed, and Israel goes around (20:20–21; 21:4). Deuteronomy 2:4–8 tells it more gently, and Deuteronomy 23:7 still says not to loathe an Edomite. The prophets later condemn Edom's violence against "your brother Jacob" (Obadiah 10).
sections.refs: Numbers 20:14–21; Numbers 21:4; Deuteronomy 2:4–8; Deuteronomy 23:7; Judges 11:17; Obadiah 10–12

sections.b: Christian readers have found several types in these chapters: the grape cluster on the pole as Christ on the cross (Numbers 13:23), Joshua's name as the name of Jesus (13:16), Aaron's blooming staff as the virgin birth or resurrection (17:8), the red heifer burned outside the camp (19:3; Hebrews 9:13; 13:11–13), the rock that was Christ (20:8–11; 1 Corinthians 10:4), and the bronze snake lifted up (21:8–9; John 3:14). The New Testament itself makes the last three links.
sections.refs: Numbers 13:16, 23; Numbers 17:8; Numbers 19:2–9; Numbers 20:8–11; Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14–15; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Hebrews 9:13–14

sections.b: Numbers 21:14 quotes "the Book of the Wars of the LORD," a lost collection of war poems, and 21:17–18 and 21:27–30 quote a well song and a victory song, probably from similar sources. A lost "Book of Eldad and Modat" is quoted in the Shepherd of Hermas (Vision 2.3.4), named after the two men who prophesied in the camp (Numbers 11:26).

When God's cloud lifts, Miriam is "struck with a skin disease, like snow" (Numbers 12:10), the same words used of Moses' hand (Exodus 4:6). Like anyone with the disease, she must stay outside the camp seven days (12:14–15; Leviticus 13:4–5). The rabbis took her case as the model of skin disease as punishment for evil speech. Aaron's plea that she not be "like one dead" (12:12) shows how the disease was felt: as a living death.

The scouts claim they saw "the Nephilim" in Canaan and felt like grasshoppers beside them (Numbers 13:33), linking the tall Anakim of Hebron with the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4. Since the flood was said to have destroyed them, many modern commentators take the claim as frightened exaggeration. The Septuagint lacks the words that link Anakim and Nephilim. Later Jewish writers took the story further, and some said Og had survived the flood.

Israel camps "facing Moab" and crosses the Zered and the Arnon, Moab's borders (Numbers 21:11–13). The Song of Heshbon mocks Moab as the "people of Chemosh," whose land Sihon took (21:26–30), and Jeremiah 48:45–46 reuses its lines. The Mesha Stele, Moab's own inscription, names Chemosh and towns from this chapter such as Dibon, Medeba and Jahaz. Moab will become the setting for the rest of the book, from Balaam's blessings to the plains where Moses speaks.

God tells Miriam and Aaron that he speaks with other prophets in visions and dreams, but with Moses "mouth to mouth, openly and not in riddles," and that Moses "looks at the form of the LORD" (Numbers 12:6–8). The Septuagint softens "form" to "glory." Paul's "now we look through a mirror, and what we see is a riddle... then we will see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12) may echo the Greek of this verse.

Korah says, "The whole community is holy" (Numbers 16:3), right after God's command "you will be holy to your God" (15:40). Moses answers that the LORD will show "who is holy" (16:5, 7). The chapter separates the holiness of all Israel from the special holiness of those God brings near to serve at the altar. Christian readers often compare 1 Peter 2:9, where all believers are "a royal priesthood."

In Numbers 14:29 God's sentence falls on "every one of you who was counted, from twenty years old and up," the men of the census of chapter 1. The second census in chapter 26 confirms that none of them but Caleb and Joshua remained (26:64–65). The rabbis held that the Levites, not counted in that census, were not under the decree.

Three places in Numbers 13–21 are often tested against archaeology. At Kadesh (13:26; 20:1), usually identified with Tell el-Qudeirat, Rudolph Cohen found Israelite forts of the 10th to 6th centuries BC but nothing earlier. Tel Arad (21:1) had a large Early Bronze Age city and an Israelite fortress, but no Late Bronze Age town. Tell Hesban, the usual site of Heshbon (21:26), has an Iron Age I village of the 12th and 11th centuries BC but no Late Bronze Age city. Readers draw different conclusions. Some see the Iron I finds at Hesban as support for an arrival around 1200 BC. Some propose other sites, such as Tel Malhata for Arad or Tell Jalul for Heshbon. Others, following scholars such as John Van Seters, think the stories were written centuries later; John Bartlett and others defend older traditions behind them.
sections.refs: Numbers 13:26; Numbers 20:1; Numbers 21:1–3, 21–30; Numbers 33:36–40; Deuteronomy 2:24–37; Judges 11:19–26

sections.b: Numbers 11 and 12 are core texts on prophecy. God takes some of the spirit on Moses and puts it on seventy elders, who prophesy once (11:25). Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses refuses to stop them: "If only all the LORD's people were prophets" (11:29). In chapter 12 God sets out degrees of revelation. Other prophets receive visions and dreams, but with Moses he speaks "mouth to mouth" (12:6–8). Jewish tradition built on this the belief that Moses' prophecy is unlike any other, and Maimonides made it a principle of faith. Joel 2:28–29 turns Moses' wish into a promise, and Acts 2:16–18 says it was fulfilled at Pentecost.
sections.refs: Numbers 11:16–29; Numbers 12:6–8; Deuteronomy 18:15–22; Deuteronomy 34:10; Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:16–18

sections.b: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married (Numbers 12:1). Whether she is Zipporah the Midianite or a second wife from Cush, south of Egypt, Moses' marriage outside Israel is the complaint's starting point, though the complaint turns at once to Moses' authority (12:2), and God takes Moses' side.
